newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Clinton urges ban on landmines, fissile material.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges ban on landmines, fissile material.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton called on Tuesday for pushing ahead with global negotiations to ban landmines and halt production of nuclear bomb-making material.
In a message to the opening 1997 session of the Conference on Disarmament, Clinton said prohibiting fissile material would contribute to the ultimate goal of total nuclear disarmament.
He urged the 61-member body to begin negotiating a global ban on anti-personnel landmines, including their use, production, stockpiling and transfer, but offered no timetable.
The White House announced last Friday that the United States would unilaterally observe a permanent ban on the export of anti-personnel landmines and seek a global ban in Geneva talks.

"These weapons of war have caused terrible suffering to innocent civilians and represent an enormous obstacle to restoring a hopeful life after a conflict has ended," Clinton said in a message read by U.S. Ambassador Stephen Ledogar.

On fissile material, plutonium and highly-enriched uranium, Clinton said: "Effectively cutting off the spigot for more nuclear weapons is a necessary step towards, and would greatly contribute to, the ultimate goal of nuclear disarmament."
Canada, which has pursued efforts to negotiate a ban through its "Ottawa process" of talks among 50 countries, said its priority was to put in place a landmine treaty by December 1997.
"The momentum towards a ban continues to grow," Canada's Disarmament Ambassador Mark Moher said in a speech.
He urged the Conference to develop a formal mandate for landmines and quickly conclude negotiations, but stressed all efforts "must be complementary and mutually reinforcing".

There are some 100 million landmines sown worldwide which kill or maim an estimated 25,000 civilians a year, including thousands of children, according to the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) which has long campaigned for a ban.
Britain's Diana, Princess of Wales called for an international ban on the "hideous weapons" when she visited Angola last week and met casualties of its 20-year civil war.
Italy's Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini appealed for a global landmine ban to be agreed within two years.
"Priority must be given to emergency situations and the main emergency the international community is required to deal with today is the question of anti-personnel landmines," he said.
"We must focus on this issue for moral and humanitarian reasons and also in the interest of economic development."
France and Britain have backed negotiations in Geneva on landmines, but major states using landmines, including China, Russia and India, have been reluctant, according to envoys.
Dini, asked how long it would take the United-Nations sponsored body to negotiate a ban on anti-personnel landmines, noted the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty had taken two years.
"I think the landmine situation is a simpler issue, in my own view, and should take less than that," he added.
Dini also urged reviving the fissile "cut off" talks.
The Geneva Conference agreed in March 1995 to negotiate a treaty to halt production of fissile material, but the talks never got off the ground as CTBT negotiations took precedence.
The forum remains divided over its 1997 agenda, according to its current chairman, South Korea's ambassador Joun Yung Sun.

India and Pakistan are leading the non-aligned countries in pushing for the five declared nuclear powers (Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States) to agree to negotiate total nuclear disarmament within a defined timetable.
Only then would the non-aligned be prepared to push ahead on cut-off as part of an overall package, according to diplomats.
But Britain on Tuesday argued against such linkage.

"In our view, the Conference on Disarmament should continue to do what it has always done best -- namely to negotiate detailed treaties on specific subjects," Sir Michael Weston said. "The CD should not now depart from this winning formula."
